rows.label: Concept
rows.text: In an elastic collision, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. In an inelastic collision, momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not (some converts to heat/sound). In a perfectly inelastic collision, the bodies stick together and KE loss is maximum. The coefficient of restitution e measures the elasticity of the collision.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Elastic collision (1D): v₁ = [(m₁−m₂)u₁ + 2m₂u₂]/(m₁+m₂); v₂ = [(m₂−m₁)u₂ + 2m₁u₁]/(m₁+m₂)
Perfectly inelastic: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁+m₂)v (common velocity v)
Coefficient of restitution: e = (v₂ − v₁)/(u₁ − u₂) = relative speed of separation / relative speed of approach

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the objects DO NOT lose ALL their kinetic energy. They lose the MAXIMUM possible KE consistent with momentum conservation. The center-of-mass kinetic energy (½Mv_cm²) MUST remain because momentum is conserved. Only the KE relative to the center of mass can be lost.  ·  The coefficient of restitution e is NOT the ratio of final to initial KE. e = (v₂ - v₁)/(u₁ - u₂) is the ratio of relative speeds. The fraction of KE retained is e² (for equal masses) or a more complex formula for unequal masses. Many students confuse e with KE ratio.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the objects do NOT lose ALL their kinetic energy — only the KE relative to the center of mass can be lost.  ·  The coefficient of restitution e depends on the materials, not on the velocities of the colliding bodies.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Equal mass elastic: A 2 kg ball at 6 m/s hits a stationary 2 kg ball. After collision: first ball stops, second ball moves at 6 m/s (velocities exchanged).  ·  Perfectly inelastic: A 3 kg ball at 4 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg ball. They stick together. Common velocity = (3×4 + 0)/(3+1) = 3 m/s. KE lost = ½×3×16 − ½×4×9 = 24 − 18 = 6 J.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Momentum is ALWAYS conserved in an isolated system (no external forces). Kinetic energy is ONLY conserved in perfectly elastic collisions. Students often think KE is always conserved in collisions — it is NOT. Real collisions are usually somewhat inelastic (0 < e < 1).  ·  For a ball bouncing on the floor: The floor/earth is so massive it doesn't move. The ball's speed before and after impact relates by e = v_after/v_before. The ball loses (1-e²) of its KE each bounce. The floor provides the impulse to change momentum; the earth's recoil is negligible.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Solve 5 one-dimensional elastic collision problems using the standard formulas.  ·  Solve 5 perfectly inelastic collision problems finding the common velocity and KE loss.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Equal mass shortcut: if m₁ = m₂ and the collision is elastic, the masses exchange velocities.  ·  Perfectly inelastic shortcut: bodies stick together → use m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v to find the common velocity.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: A 4 kg ball moving at 5 m/s collides elastically with a 2 kg ball at rest. Find their velocities after collision.  ·  A 5 kg ball moving at 6 m/s hits a stationary 3 kg ball in a perfectly inelastic collision. Find the common velocity and the KE lost.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: One-dimensional elastic collision formulas are standard — know how to derive and apply them.  ·  Equal-mass elastic collision (one at rest): the moving mass stops, the stationary one moves off at the original speed.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: In an elastic collision, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.  ·  In an inelastic collision, momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not (some converts to heat/sound).  ·  In a perfectly inelastic collision, the bodies stick together and KE loss is maximum.  ·  The coefficient of restitution e = (relative speed of separation)/(relative speed of approach).

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Elastic collision: both momentum AND kinetic energy are conserved.  ·  Inelastic collision: momentum conserved, kinetic energy NOT conserved (some → heat/sound).  ·  Perfectly inelastic: bodies stick together, KE loss is maximum.  ·  Coefficient of restitution e = 1 (elastic), e = 0 (perfectly inelastic), 0 < e < 1 (inelastic).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The coefficient of restitution e was introduced by Newton in the Principia. For elastic collisions, e = 1, and the relative velocity of separation equals the relative velocity of approach. This is a consequence of both momentum and kinetic energy conservation.  ·  In any isolated system, total momentum is ALWAYS conserved (if no external forces). Kinetic energy is NOT always conserved. The only perfectly elastic collisions in nature are between fundamental particles (or at the atomic/molecular level where quantum mechanics makes collisions elastic).

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: A ball is dropped from 10 m and rebounds to 6.4 m. Find the coefficient of restitution and the fraction of energy lost.  ·  A 1 kg ball moving at 8 m/s collides with a stationary 4 kg ball. If e = 0.6, find the final velocities.  ·  Explain why the ball in a golf shot travels faster than the club head.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Perfectly inelastic collision: find the common velocity using momentum conservation, then compute KE loss.  ·  Coefficient of restitution problems: e = (v₂ − v₁)/(u₁ − u₂) — just the ratio of relative speeds.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Coefficient of restitution: A ball dropped from 5 m rebounds to 3.2 m. e = √(3.2/5) = 0.8.  ·  Golf club: A 0.2 kg club at 50 m/s hits a 0.046 kg ball at rest (e = 0.8). Ball speed = 73.2 m/s (faster than the club!).

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s hits a stationary 2 kg ball in an elastic collision. The final velocity of the first ball is: → A  ·  A 3 kg ball moving at 4 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg ball in a perfectly inelastic collision. Their common velocity is: → A

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Elastic collision:** A collision in which both total momentum AND total kinetic energy are conserved. The bodies rebound without permanent deformation, no sound/heat is produced. The relative velocity of approach equals the relative velocity of separation: v₂ - v₁ = u₁ - u₂.  ·  **Inelastic collision:** A collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is NOT conserved. Some kinetic energy is converted to internal energy (heat, sound, deformation). The coefficient of restitution e < 1.  ·  **Perfectly inelastic collision:** The extreme case where the colliding bodies stick together after collision and move with a common velocity. Momentum is conserved; KE loss is maximum (but not 100% because momentum must be conserved, so some KE remains as center-of-mass motion).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: In the center-of-mass frame, total momentum is zero — simplifies collision analysis.  ·  KE loss in inelastic collision: ΔK = ½μv_rel²(1 − e²), where μ = m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂)  ·  Equal mass elastic (one at rest): v₁ = 0, v₂ = u₁ (velocities exchanged)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Equal-mass elastic collision (one at rest): the masses exchange velocities.  ·  A collision where kinetic energy is 'gained' (superelastic) is possible if internal energy is released (explosion, chemical reaction, spring release). These are NOT standard collisions and require tracking internal energy changes.  ·  Newton's cradle: Pull one ball, release — one ball flies out the other end at the same speed. Pull two balls, two fly out.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: In an elastic collision between equal masses where one is initially at rest, the masses exchange velocities.  ·  Momentum is conserved in ALL collisions (elastic and inelastic) as long as no external force acts.  ·  NEB collision problems: always check whether the collision is elastic (use both conservation laws) or inelastic (use only momentum conservation).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: In an elastic collision, both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved.  ·  In an inelastic collision, momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not — some converts to internal energy.  ·  In a perfectly inelastic collision, the colliding bodies stick together and move with a common velocity.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: In the center-of-mass frame, total momentum is zero — this simplifies collision analysis.  ·  KE loss shortcut: ΔK = ½μv_rel²(1 − e²) — maximum when e = 0 (perfectly inelastic).  ·  e = 1 → elastic (KE conserved); e = 0 → perfectly inelastic (maximum KE loss); 0 < e < 1 → inelastic.
